name: New Product Launch Presentation
description: A cinematic dark product-launch keynote in black, white, and electric blue, introducing the market shift, product position, experience and technology, rollout plan, launch metrics, editions, pricing, and availability.
style_guide:
# New Product Launch Presentation

## Purpose

Create a high-impact launch narrative that explains why the market is changing, what the new product is, who it is for, how the experience works, why the technology matters, how the launch unfolds, and what customers can buy and when. This is a keynote, not an internal roadmap or feature inventory. Preview products, specifications, claims, prices, dates, and availability are fictional.

## Visual signature

Use a full dark environment with white typography, electric-blue accents, cool gray support, and subtle technical grid lines. Large product statements dominate; compact panels and diagrams carry proof. The design should feel precise and cinematic without glow-heavy gaming effects. Keep each slide focused on one reveal.

## Canvas and composition

- Fixed 16:9 canvas with `100–130 px` margins and a 12-column grid.
- Use one primary statement, diagram, or timeline per page. Preserve 30–45 percent negative space.
- Prefer `7/5` statement-and-diagram splits, three benefit panels, a central technology map, and a full-width launch sequence.
- Panels have square corners, low-contrast borders, and no conventional shadows.
- Avoid placing more than six discrete product facts on a main slide.

## Colors

- Launch black `#070A0F`: dominant background.
- Panel charcoal `#111827`: technical panels and price fields.
- White `#F8FAFC`: titles and important values.
- Electric blue `#2476FF`: product identity, active layer, phase, and CTA.
- Cool gray `#8B95A7`: supporting copy.
- Grid line `#1B2638`: subtle structure.
- Any additional edition or status color must be muted and secondary to electric blue.

## Typography

Use `Inter`, `Space Grotesk`, `Aptos`, or `Arial` for the full deck; optionally use `IBM Plex Mono` for specs, event labels, versions, and availability. Cover title `62–82 px`; body reveal `42–58 px`; hero value `52–72 px`; panel title `20–27 px`; body `13–18 px`; technical label `10–12 px`. Use short lines and deliberate breaks.

## Page archetypes

### 1. Cover and launch-event context

Use a near-black field, one electric-blue line or edge, product category label, launch title, short promise, event or audience context, date, and presenter. Do not show unapproved specs or pricing.

### 2. Market shift and launch theme

Frame two or three verified shifts with evidence, then state the launch theme as the product response. Distinguish market data from company interpretation and avoid declaring a new era without substantiation.

### 3. Product positioning and value proposition

State the target audience, category, problem, differentiated promise, and three outcome-led benefits. The product name should support the promise rather than replace it. Each benefit requires a mechanism or proof path.

### 4. Technology and experience demonstration

Use an experience flow or system map connecting user action, interface behavior, enabling technology, and visible outcome. Show only launch-ready capabilities. Label simulated demonstrations, prototypes, future features, and required dependencies.

### 5. Go-to-market rollout and launch metrics

Use three phases such as announce, activate, and scale. Show audience, channel, milestone, owner, inventory or capacity dependency, and launch KPI for each phase. Separate operational readiness from market performance.

### 6. Editions, pricing, and availability

Present no more than three editions or purchase options with consistent included capabilities, limits, price basis, market, availability date, and CTA. Identify taxes, subscription term, hardware requirements, regional exceptions, and planned versus confirmed availability.

## Product-claim integrity

All performance, speed, battery, privacy, compatibility, AI, environmental, and benchmark claims need an approved source and test conditions. Do not invent launch dates, availability, certifications, reviews, customer quotes, or comparative superiority. Keep roadmap items out of launch-ready lists. If a demo is simulated, disclose it on the page.

## Avoid

Do not use gradients, neon glow, lens flares, particle fields, 3D mockups without approved assets, dense spec tables, or generic futuristic imagery. Do not claim category leadership without a defined market and source. Do not make pricing or availability ambiguous.
